summary: Describes an in-band data communication network for the MPLS Transport Profile. It uses the Generic Associated Channel to carry management and control traffic along the same paths as user data. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Trains can carry a small mail car alongside passengers. This lets network equipment send its own control messages through the same channel as normal traffic, with no separate wiring.

subtitle: How MPLS-TP nodes with no IP links can still carry their own management and signaling messages.

tldr.problem: Some MPLS-TP nodes have no IP on their line-side interfaces and no separate out-of-fiber network, yet their management and control protocols still need a way to talk.
tldr.mechanism: Management and signaling messages are wrapped in a Generic Associated Channel (G-ACh) header whose Channel Type says Management Communication Channel (MCC) or Signaling Communication Channel (SCC), plus a two-byte PID naming the payload protocol.
tldr.outcome: The result is an in-band Data Communication Network (DCN) built from MPLS labels. It is meant only for networks that cannot carry native DCN messages, and the protocols on top must bring their own security.

today: RFC 5718 is a Proposed Standard from January 2010. The metadata for this RFC lists no obsoleting or updating documents.

sections.title: Why an In-Band DCN Is Needed
sections.content:
MPLS Label Switching Routers (LSRs) are normally managed with management protocols or control plane protocols, and those protocols usually exchange IP packets. Some nodes in an MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) network are built without support for direct IP encapsulation on their line-side interfaces and have no access to an out-of-fiber data communication network. For these nodes the only available mechanism is an MPLS label.

The Generic Associated Channel (G-ACh) from RFC 5586 generalizes the pseudowire associated channel header from RFC 4385 so it can be used on any MPLS Label Switched Path (LSP). This document defines how the G-ACh builds a Management Communication Network (MCN) and a Signaling Communication Network (SCN), together called the Data Communication Network (DCN).

The G-ACh is intended to provide DCN connectivity only where the MPLS-TP network cannot encapsulate or deliver native DCN messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Some network boxes cannot send ordinary control messages because they have no normal mailbox for them. So they use a special lane inside the traffic they already carry.

sections.title: Requirements From the ITU-T
sections.content:
The requirements were communicated to the IETF by the ITU-T. In short:

  • A packet-encapsulation mechanism must carry MCN and SCN packets over the G-ACh.
  • It must work between two adjacent MPLS-TP nodes, and also when an MPLS-TP tunnel crosses another operator's domain (the carrier's carrier scenario).
  • The G-ACh must give two independent channels, an MCC for the MCN and an SCC for the SCN, so that packets can be handed to the management or the control plane. This also allows separate or overlapping address spaces and duplicate protocol instances.
  • Separate rate limiters and traffic shapers per channel must not be ruled out, though they are outside the scope of the definitions.
  • The channel must be able to carry IPv4, IPv6 and OSI PDUs, and the header must say which one is inside.

The G-ACh itself is not required to provide security mechanisms, but the protocols running over the MCC or SCC must.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules say there must be two separate lanes, one for management notes and one for control notes, and that each note says what language it is written in.

sections.title: The MCC/SCC Packet Format
sections.content:
To send a DCN message, the sender prepends an Associated Channel Header (ACH) to it. The Channel Type field says whether the message is an MCC or an SCC message. The ACH MUST NOT include the ACH TLV Header from RFC 5586, so no ACH TLVs can be included.

The presence of a two-byte Protocol Identifier (PID) field is deduced from the Channel Type value. The PID identifies the payload protocol using the PPP protocol identifiers from RFC 1661 and RFC 3818. The first four bits of the header are 0001, followed by a Version field and a Reserved field.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note gets a small label on the front. One part says which lane it belongs to, and another says what kind of message is inside.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving
sections.content:
The sender creates the G-ACh header, sets the Channel Type to MCC (or SCC for a control plane message), fills in the PID for the layer 3 PDU type and prepends the header to the message.

If the G-ACh is associated with an MPLS section, the Generic Associated Channel Label (GAL) is added to the message. If it is associated with an LSP, the GAL is added and the LSP label is pushed on top of it. In both cases the GAL's TTL MUST be 1 and its S-bit MUST be 1. The normal handling of the Traffic Class (TC) field still applies, so it could be used to prioritize different DCN packets.

A receiver looks at the PID. If it knows the value, it delivers the message to the right processing entity. If not, it SHALL silently discard the packet, and MAY count the discard or log an event. Per RFC 5586, a receiver MUST NOT forward a GAL packet based on the GAL label.

The DCN channel MUST NOT carry user traffic and SHALL only carry management or control plane messages. Nodes are not required to support IP or OSI forwarding in the fast path, so protocols using the DCN should not assume forwarding capabilities unless these are known beforehand or learned through a routing protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender sticks on the label and marks it as a one-hop note. The receiver reads the label, hands the note to the right helper, and quietly throws away notes it does not understand.

sections.title: Applicability and Pseudowire Setup
sections.content:
The DCN links management stations to network nodes and nodes to each other. Appendix A of the MPLS-TP network management requirements describes control channels that can be out-of-fiber and out-of-band, in-fiber and out-of-band, or in-band. Used as described here, the G-ACh yields a "data channel associated CCh" (type 6), tied to an MPLS-TP section, and an "in-band CCh" (type 7), tied to an MPLS-TP LSP or PW that may span several hops.

There is no need to create a channel for every LSP between a pair of nodes. Physically adjacent nodes would normally use the section G-ACh. For nodes connected by LSP tunnels, one or two LSPs might be chosen to provide the channel and a back-up.

Provider Edge nodes that want to set up pseudowires with a signaling protocol using remote adjacencies, such as LDP (RFC 5036), MUST first set up an LSP tunnel when there is no IP-based control network. That tunnel carries the pseudowire and also provides the G-ACh-based DCN between the PEs.
sections.plainLanguage: Neighbors next door use the direct lane. Nodes farther apart pick one or two tunnels to be the message lane, with a spare in case one breaks.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The G-ACh provides a virtual link between MPLS-TP nodes and might be used to induce many forms of security attack. The MPLS data plane has no security mechanisms of its own, so protocols using the DCN are REQUIRED to include adequate security mechanisms, and implementations MUST let operators configure their use.

IANA allocated two Channel Types from the PW Associated Channel Type registry defined in RFC 4446 and updated by RFC 5586: 0x0001 for the MCC and 0x0002 for the SCC.
sections.plainLanguage: The special lane has no lock of its own, so whoever uses it has to bring their own lock. Two lane numbers were reserved so everyone agrees which is which.
